papers.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response.
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's κ, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (κ range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

papers.title: Sleep-like slow waves in wakefulness index post-stroke behavioural alterations.
papers.abstract: Increases in high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep serve as markers of neuronal silencing, which disrupts functional connectivity and is associated with a loss of awareness and responsiveness. Cortical slowing likewise occurs during wakefulness, upon sleep deprivation, and accompanies performance deterioration. Recent work has revealed similar oscillations (termed 'sleep-like slow waves') following stroke in brain regions close or connected to a brain lesion, offering a plausible but untested mechanism for stroke-related behavioural impairment. Here, we simultaneously recorded EEG and behavioural performance while 30 unilateral stroke patients (12 left hemisphere, 18 right hemisphere) and 27 age-matched healthy adults completed a computerised perceptual decision-making task. Stroke patients had predominantly middle cerebral artery strokes (n=25), with a small subset of posterior cerebral artery (n=4), and anterior cerebral artery/middle cerebral artery (n=1) lesions. Sleep-like slow waves occurred more frequently in stroke patients relative to healthy controls, with limited spatial specificity when comparing patients with left and right lesion sites (more slow waves ipsilateral of the lesion). Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between slow wave occurrence and the accuracy and speed of perceptual reports in stroke patients, suggesting that variations in the occurrence of slow waves may contribute to cognitive heterogeneity post-stroke. As sleep-like slow waves predict deficits in perceptual decision-making following stroke, they represent a plausible mechanism of post-lesion functional network dysfunction extending beyond the damaged regions, thereby contributing to broader cognitive impairments.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3±1% with a false positive rate of 6.0±0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R 2 =0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Eight decades after Leão's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Optimized phase-targeted auditory stimulation reduces nocturnal spikes in childhood epilepsies
papers.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges, so called spikes, are often strongly activated during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in childhood epilepsies. In children with pronounced spike activation during NREM - sleep, spike burden can be associated with lifelong impaired cognitive functions. This spike activation is also related to alterations in sleep oscillations, specifically slow waves and spindles, which play essential roles in brain maintenance and maturation. These observations suggest that spikes may disrupt sleep-dependent brain processes that are critical for the development of cognitive functions. Phase-targeted auditory stimulation during NREM sleep delivers brief, non-arousing tones at specific phases of ongoing slow waves to modulate sleep oscillations. Recently, our group showed that isolated, less frequent, and thus less expected, tones engage widespread thalamocortical networks, whereas repetitive, regular trains of tones promote habituation and engage more local corticocortical networks. In this study, we use these contrasting stimulation patterns for a targeted modulation of sleep oscillations and examine their interaction with epileptic spikes. In an initial exploratory study (N = 10; age range: 7.3 - 16.2 years), we used a within-night block design to directly compare responses to the different stimulation patterns. Isolated tones delivered at long interstimulus intervals induced a transient increase in spike rate, whereas down-phase stimulation delivered in trains at short, regular intervals was associated with a significant reduction. We subsequently optimized the train-based paradigm and evaluated stimulation delivered throughout the night in a proof-of-concept study using a counterbalanced, between-night design (N = 5; age range: 4.4 - 10.7 years). Spike density decreased locally in all patients, providing convergent evidence for the effects observed in the exploratory study. With this mechanistically guided approach, we demonstrate that repetitive down-phase auditory stimulation of slow waves results in a local reduction of epileptic spikes. This framework may provide a rational basis for targeted interventions aimed at reducing spikes and related cognitive impairments.

papers.title: EEG-based deep learning estimates preterm infants' cerebral age: Contribution of slow-wave and cross-frequency coupling.
papers.abstract: Reliably estimating cerebral maturation in preterm newborns is crucial for early identification of atypical neurodevelopment. We developed a deep-learning framework using a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict postmenstrual age (PMA) from spontaneous neural activity in EEG recordings of 165 healthy preterm infants (28-38 weeks PMA). The model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.75 ± 0.60 weeks, with 73.9% of prediction errors within one week. To identify key neurophysiological drivers, we systematically manipulated signal components. Results showed that removing low-frequency activity (<4 Hz) significantly degraded performance and disrupting phase-amplitude coupling selectively impaired prediction accuracy before 34 weeks PMA, while high-frequency activity (>12 Hz) had minimal impact. Our results demonstrate that maturation signatures are primarily driven by slow-wave dynamics and their hierarchical coupling with faster oscillations, which are fundamental hallmarks of early neurodevelopment.

papers.title: How Does Sleep Deprivation Rewrite the Cognitive Function in the Hippocampus?
papers.abstract: In the modern society, sleep loss has become a global concern. Sleep deprivation (SD), a special type of complete acute or chronic sleep loss, swiftly erodes cognitive functions with observed structural and functional changes in the brain according to previous research. Hippocampus, especially its cornu ammonis 1 region presenting density in cognition-critical pyramidal neurons and complex inter-cellular crosstalk, is particularly vulnerable to sleep loss. SD disrupts hippocampal structure and function, leading to cognitive deficits. Mechanistically, by uncoupling energy-redox homeostasis, SD silences plasticity-promoting signals and neuron-glia interactions while amplifying neuroinflammation and metabolic deficits, thereby disrupting synaptic efficacy, network synchrony, waste removal procedure, and neurogenesis across the hippocampus and its related circuits. Although several pharmacological and non-pharmacological translational attempts have been announced, more efforts are in demand for advanced multi-modal models and cohorts integrating transcriptomics, connectomics, and real-time neuromodulation for elucidating the cascading mechanisms of SD-induced cognitive deficits in the hippocampus, as well as for interventions restoring sleep-dependent cognitive resilience and supporting precision psychiatry.

papers.title: Sleep complaints in alexithymia reflect non-specific negative affectivity.
papers.abstract: Alexithymia is the inability to identify and describe emotions, associated with an increased risk of somatic and psychiatric disease. Alexithymia is also characterized by reduced subjective sleep quality. However, it is not well-known if this reduction in sleep quality reflects physiological changes in sleep, a specific alteration in perceived sleep quality not captured by objective metrics, or a non-specific spillover of the negative affective style which characterizes alexithymia. In BSETS, a large (N = 228) in-home EEG study of naturalistic sleep, we found that alexithymia symptoms are associated with worse habitual (AIS) and current (GSQS) subjective sleep quality (βAIS = 0.207, pAIS = 0.002, βGSQS = 0.203, pGSQS = 0.002). However, we observed no significant association between alexithymia and EEG-based sleep efficiency (β = -0.017, p = 0.791). The association with subjective sleep quality was almost completely attenuated when controlling for either depressive symptoms (PHQ-9, βAIS = 0.001, pAIS = 0.982, βGSQS = 0.044, pGSQS = 0.486) or trait neuroticism (ZKPQ, BFI-44, βAIS = 0.057, pAIS = 0.442, βGSQS = 0.048, pGSQS = 0.514). A possible exception is the Difficulty Identifying Feelings alexithymia dimension, reflecting complaints about the labeling of interoceptive experiences, which was associated with lower subjective sleep quality even after covariate control. This pattern of findings suggests that alexithymia is characterized only by alterations of subjective sleep quality, and even these reflect a non-specific increase in negative affect which influences self-reports of sleep quality, rather than a specific reduction in perceived sleep quality itself.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Spectral Power in Young Adults With Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Self-Reported Habitual Short Sleep: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and insufficient sleep frequently co-occur during early adulthood, yet resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) evidence in this population remains limited. The present study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG spectral power in young adults with GAD who also reported habitual short sleep, compared with healthy controls. This exploratory case-control study included 56 university students: 28 participants with GAD and self-reported habitual short sleep and 28 healthy controls. Resting-state EEG spectral power was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. We retained unadjusted group comparisons for description and fitted age- and sex-adjusted linear models for the primary inferential interpretation. Channel-wise models likewise included group, age, and sex, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the 30 channels within each frequency band. After adjustment for age and sex, group coefficients remained positive for delta (2.51, 95% CI: 0.20 to 4.82), theta (2.52, 95% CI: 0.29 to 4.74), alpha (2.46, 95% CI: -0.12 to 5.03), and beta power (2.14, 95% CI: 0.13 to 4.15), but none met the FDR threshold (adjusted FDR p = 0.0501, 0.0501, 0.0608, and 0.0501, respectively). In unadjusted analyses, delta, theta, and beta differences survived FDR correction (FDR p = 0.0480 for each), whereas alpha did not (FDR p = 0.0553). In adjusted channel-wise analyses, 26 channel-by-band comparisons across 15 channels survived within-band FDR correction; all occurred in delta or theta and were concentrated over posterior and centroparietal electrodes. Whole-scalp estimates were directionally higher in the GAD plus habitual short-sleep group, but no age- and sex-adjusted frequency-band comparison survived FDR correction. Adjusted exploratory channel-wise findings indicated a posterior and centroparietal concentration in delta and theta power. These estimates remain preliminary and do not permit attribution to GAD, habitual short sleep, or their interaction.

papers.title: Impact of Combined Chronic Stress and REM Sleep Deprivation on Memory Function and Hippocampal BDNF Protein Content in Wistar Rats.
papers.abstract: The concurrent impact of chronic psychological stress and sleep disruption on systemic adaptation and hippocampal cytoarchitecture remains poorly understood. This study investigated the neurobiological threshold of compounded stress by exposing male Wistar rats to combined Chronic Unpredictable Mild Stress (CUMS) and Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Deprivation (RSD), specifically chosen over total sleep deprivation due to the unique role of REM sleep in emotional regulation and spatial memory consolidation over 21 days. We evaluated body weight loss, sensorimotor function Open Field Test (OFT), declarative memory Novel Object Recognition (NOR), serum corticosterone, hippocampal malondialdehyde (MDA), and Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF). Results revealed that the combined stress paradigm precipitated significant body weight loss while preserving basal locomotor activity. In contrast to motor preservation, spatial recognition memory was significantly impaired. Biochemically, serum corticosterone and hippocampal MDA levels did not show statistically significant differences across groups. Crucially, while isolated CUMS significantly suppressed hippocampal BDNF protein content and RSD exhibited a similar trend of reduction, the combined paradigm triggered a compensatory neurotrophic rebound, returning BDNF to control baseline levels. However, the localized BDNF rebound did not translate to recovery cognitive performance. These findings suggest a phenomenon of neurobiological dissociation under compounded stress exposure. The organism experiences significant body weight loss and declarative memory impairment, while simultaneously initiating a localized, yet functionally ineffective, compensatory BDNF response in the hippocampus.

papers.title: CK2 and DBT promote temperature compensation of the Drosophila circadian clock via distinct pathways.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are defined by three fundamental properties: they are self-sustained, entrained by environmental cues, and temperature compensated. The molecular basis of temperature compensation remains incompletely understood. Here, we found that reducing the activity of two highly conserved circadian kinases, Drosophila doubletime/casein kinase 1 and casein kinase 2 (DBT/CK1 and CK2), compromises temperature compensation in Drosophila melanogaster. Genetic analyses indicate that DBT and CK2 promote temperature compensation through distinct but additive pathways. DBT works through the per Short phosphorylation cluster and the Ser47 phosphodegron of the core clock protein PER, whereas CK2 acts through a phosphocluster in TIM and PER Ser45 residue. Simultaneous disruption of both pathways results in hyperphosphorylated PER accumulation and impaired PER clearance from circadian pacemaker neuron nuclei. Combined with previous studies, our findings support a central role for nuclear PER phosphorylation dynamics in buffering circadian period against environmental temperature fluctuations.

papers.title: Loss of PEA-15 Alters ERK/MAPK Signaling and Circadian Function in the Suprachiasmatic Nucleus.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are a fundamental biological process that coordinates physiological functions, behavior, and metabolism with an approximately 24-hour periodicity. At the center of the mammalian circadian timing system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which generates robust, clock-gated neuronal output that establishes the temporal organization of cellular and physiological processes throughout the body. Our previous work demonstrated that the scaffold protein PEA-15 (phosphoprotein enriched in astrocytes 15) is highly expressed in the SCN and dynamically interacts with ERK, a key effector kinase of the MAPK pathway, to regulate its subcellular localization. Given the important role of ERK/MAPK signaling in circadian timing and photic entrainment, we extended this work using PEA-15 knockout (PEA-15 -/- ) mice to determine how loss of PEA- 15 affects circadian timing, entrainment, and ERK signaling within the SCN. At the cellular level, both clock-gated and light-evoked ERK activation were significantly reduced in PEA- 15 -/- mice compared with wild-type controls. Under constant darkness, PEA-15 -/- mice exhibited a significantly shorter free-running period relative to wild-type animals. Assessment of circadian entrainment using jet-lag resetting and Aschoff type I light-pulse paradigms revealed a blunted phase-delay response to light and an accelerated rate of entrainment to a phase-advancing light stimulus. Thus, loss of PEA-15 alters multiple properties of the SCN clock, including its intrinsic period and its responsiveness to photic input, with effects that depend on the direction of phase resetting. Collectively, these findings identify PEA-15 as an important regulator of SCN circadian function and implicate ERK/MAPK signaling as one mechanism through which PEA-15 modulates clock timing and photic entrainment.

papers.title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
papers.abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

They propose that light-induced shifts in GABAergic excitation/inhibition balance, driven by chloride cotransporter expression changes, flip ipsilateral and contralateral coupling signs so that left and right shell populations oscillate in antiphase, reproducing splitting, unilateral lesion effects, and experimental data.

papers.title: Rest-activity rhythm fragmentation, functional limitation, and mortality in adults with arthritis: A nationally representative cohort study.
papers.abstract: To characterize rest-activity rhythms in adults with arthritis, examine the role of functional limitation, and evaluate whether rhythm fragmentation is associated with mortality. We analyzed 7920 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) with at least 4 valid days of wrist accelerometry; arthritis status was available for 7904, including 2182 with arthritis. Nonparametric rest-activity rhythm features were evaluated using weighted linear and Cox models with primary-sampling-unit-clustered robust standard errors. Sensitivity analyses examined cohort selection and quadratic self-reported and device-estimated sleep duration. After demographic and clinical adjustment, arthritis was associated with higher intradaily variability (β = 0.063 SD, 95% CI 0.016-0.110) and lower most-active 10-hour (M10) activity (β = -0.030, 95% CI -0.051 to -0.009; both q = 0.028). Functional-limitation adjustment attenuated the intradaily variability difference (β = 0.005). Each 1-SD higher intradaily variability was associated with all-cause mortality after full adjustment (HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.10-1.26). Estimates were similar across alternative sleep-duration specifications and within participants with arthritis (HR 1.19, 95% CI 1.01-1.39). papers.title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists.
papers.abstract: Circadian physiology coordinates systemic and cellular metabolism through a light-entrained central clock and metabolically synchronized peripheral clocks. Here, we profiled colorectal cancer (CRC) responses to PPAR antagonists across 2D and 3D CRC models and tumor-bearing mice. In standard high-glucose, low-fat medium, Bmal1 oscillations and daily variation in PPAR antagonist sensitivity were apparent in CRC cells. By contrast, nutrient-defined media that recapitulate feeding and nighttime fasting abolished time-dependent variability and unified drug responses across models. Still, the fed state selectively sensitized spheroids and patient-derived organoids to PPAR-γ antagonism. In mice, dosing PPAR-γ antagonist in the fed state prolonged survival and reduced hepatotoxicity. The use of Bmal-1-silenced CRC cells validated that feeding-fasting rhythms, not tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern CRC sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. Our study also supports the predictive capacity of nutrient-alternating 3D tumor models, enabling metabolism-targeted anticancer treatment evaluation.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Wearable and Biological Data Integration Reveals Physiological Signatures of Weight Variation in Overweight and Obese Adults: An AI4Food Machine Learning Study

A 30-day crossover intervention was conducted on 93 participants at IMDEA Nutrition Institute, combining a traditional phase (questionnaires, food diaries) and a digital phase (Fitbit Sense Smartwatch, FreeStyle Libre 2 glucose sensor). The collected data encompassed sleep, glucose, skin temperature, nutrition, and gut microbiome information. After rigorous preprocessing and alignment by intervention days, unsupervised clustering, association analysis, and machine learning models were applied to uncover physiological patterns linked to weight dynamics. Results showed greater weight reduction during the digital phase in Group 2, while between-group differences were not significant. Significant associations were observed between nocturnal respiratory rate, skin temperature, and weight variation. Under participant-level five-fold cross-validation, Random Forest models achieved mean accuracies of 64.3% for thermoregulation and 61.7% for glucose phenotype prediction, with RMSSD, restlessness, and nocturnal respiratory rate among the most influential predictors. In contrast, microbiome composition remained almost stable over the short intervention period. These findings support the potential of AI-driven integration of wearable and nutritional data to stratify metabolic phenotypes and advance personalized nutrition strategies in obesity management.

papers.title: Enlightening pregnancy as a potential pathway to protect maternal circadian functioning and postpartum mood.
papers.abstract: The perinatal period is characterized by profound psychological, physiological, and behavioral changes that may increase sleep, circadian, and affective disturbances. While sleep disruption across pregnancy and postpartum has been widely documented, far less is known about how this transition shapes circadian health and whether circadian characteristics during pregnancy predict postpartum circadian and affective outcomes. In this study, we characterize circadian preference, circadian phase, circadian function, and light exposure across the transition from late pregnancy to early postpartum, and examine their predictive value for postpartum circadian function and depressive and anxiety symptomatology. Women were followed from the third trimester of pregnancy to 1 month postpartum. At both time points, participants wore a wrist actigraph to derive circadian parameters including the circadian function index (CFI) and circadian phase (L5c), and to quantify mean light exposure. Circadian preference and affective states were also assessed by questionnaires (MEQ, EPDS, STAI-T). Within-subject changes from pregnancy to postpartum were examined, and regression models were used to test whether prenatal circadian and affective measures predicted postpartum circadian function and depressive symptomatology. The transition to postpartum was marked by a significant reduction in CFI and mean light exposure, whereas circadian preference and L5c remained largely stable. During pregnancy, higher CFI was associated with morningness and greater light exposure; however, these associations were no longer evident postpartum. Postpartum CFI was predicted by prenatal CFI and circadian preference, with lower values observed among women with more evening-oriented profiles. In parallel, prenatal affective symptoms showed continuity into the postpartum period, and both prenatal CFI and circadian preference contributed to the prediction of postpartum depressive symptoms. Together, these findings indicate that early postpartum is characterized by a decay in circadian function rather than a shift in circadian phase, identify eveningness as a vulnerability factor during the transition to motherhood, support the use of CFI as an integrative marker of maternal circadian health, and highlight pregnancy as a potential window for circadian-informed interventions aimed at improving postpartum circadian and mood outcomes.

papers.title: Electroencephalography-based machine learning models for hyperacute detection of large vessel occlusion stroke.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has shown potential as a prehospital triage instrument for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (LVO-a) stroke. In this study, we determined the diagnostic accuracy of EEG-based machine learning algorithms for LVO-a stroke detection. Anterior circulation large vessel occlusion stroke detection machine learning models were developed using EEG data from the ELECTRA-STROKE (NCT03699397) and AI-STROKE (NCT05437237) studies. Single 2- to 3-min EEG recordings were obtained using 8 dry electrodes in adults with suspected stroke in prehospital and in-hospital settings. Patients with a clean EEG segment of ≥ 5 s (visually selected) were included and EEG symmetry features were extracted. We assessed the performance of multiple machine learning models using nested cross-validation (CV), optimising models with 3-fold CV (inner loop) and evaluating them with leave-one-out CV (outer loop). Of 1293 patients with suspected stroke, 336 (26%) were included (74% prehospital, 26% in-hospital). Median age was 72 (IQR 61-80) years, and 231 (69%) were male. Sixteen (5%) patients had LVO-a stroke, 140 (42%) non-LVO-a ischaemic stroke, 52 (15%) TIA, 13 (4%) haemorrhagic stroke and 115 (34%) a stroke mimic. Naïve Bayes achieved the highest observed area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.85 [95% CI, 0.77-0.93]), with a sensitivity of 69% (95% CI, 44%-86%) and specificity of 86% (95% CI, 82%-89%). Machine learning models for LVO-a stroke detection based solely on EEG showed moderately high diagnostic accuracy. These results support the potential of EEG-based LVO-a stroke detection, but improved EEG data acquisition is needed before clinical implementation can be considered.

papers.title: Disrupted cortical signatures of response inhibition in Parkinson's disease revealed by TMS-EEG.
papers.abstract: Inhibitory control deficits are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD), particularly in patients with L-DOPA-induced dyskinesias (LID), but the cortical mechanisms underlying impaired inhibition remain poorly understood. Thirty-six PD patients (18 LID-PD, 18 nLID-PD) and 20 healthy volunteers performed a Go/NoGo task during TMS-EEG, which assessed functional connectivity between the supplementary motor area (SMA) and primary motor cortex (M1), and cortical reactivity through TMS-evoked potentials. Healthy volunteers exhibited task-dependent modulation of SMA-M1 connectivity, with increased theta-band coupling during NoGo trials and gamma-band coupling during Go trials; this pattern was absent in both PD groups, particularly in those with dyskinesias. TMS-evoked potentials revealed enhanced N100 responses during NoGo trials in healthy volunteers, reduced in non-dyskinetic patients and absent in dyskinetic ones. SMA-M1 gamma connectivity correlated with motor performance and clinical severity. During post-TMS epochs, healthy volunteers showed context-dependent alpha/beta modulation that was disrupted in PD patients. papers.title: Squalamine prevents motor and non-motor symptoms in the paraquat and lectin rat model of the body-first subtype of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Increasing evidence supports the existence of a distinct body-first subtype of Parkinson's disease (PD), in which the initial site of pathology is in the gut. Animal models that recapitulate the body-first subtype of PD are needed. We tested the hypothesis that non-motor features of the body-first subtype of PD are recapitulated in the paraquat and lectin (P + L) rat model of PD, a model that has previously demonstrated the pathological motor progression of this subtype of PD. Then, we tested whether oral squalamine, a gastrointestinal prokinetic that has been shown to reduce formation of pathological α-synuclein, could prevent pathology, motor, and non-motor findings. Rats (n = 93) were orally gavaged for seven days with paraquat (1 mg/kg) and lectin (0.05%) in 1% sucrose solution. A subset of rats (n = 37) were given 30 days of squalamine (20 mg/kg) in their drinking water immediately following P + L treatment. Rats were tested for parkinsonian motor deficits, gastrointestinal dysmotility, sleep abnormalities, and cognitive deficits. Rats were euthanized and their brains processed for phospho-S129-α-synuclein pathology and neurodegeneration. We show that the P + L rat model recapitulates non-motor features and pathology of gastrointestinal dysmotility and sleep abnormalities seen in the body-first subtype of PD. We show that oral squalamine prevents motor deficits, gastrointestinal dysmotility, and sleep abnormalities, and diminishes phospho-S129-α-synuclein pathology and neurodegeneration in the nigrostriatal pathway. We show that the P + L rat model recapitulates many features of the body-first subtype of PD and provides pre-clinical evidence for the use of squalamine to mitigate progression in the body-first subtype of PD.

papers.title: Pathophysiology of REM sleep behaviour disorder.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by loss of muscle atonia and dream enactment behaviour during REM sleep. RBD is recognized as a significant prodromal marker of α-synucleinopathies, but characterizing its unique neuropathological features is challenging due to reliance on individual case reports. Additionally, RBD is not a terminal illness, and data generalisability is limited by the high co-occurrence of α-synucleinopathies. In this review, we discuss the mechanisms responsible for altered REM sleep regulation in RBD, incorporating evidence from human post-mortem histological analyses, structural and functional neuroimaging data on patients with RBD, and pharmacological studies. We explore the risks, biomarkers, and mechanisms of phenoconversion from RBD to α-synucleinopathies, drawing on data from large longitudinal patient cohorts, and we consider disease remission. Lastly, we propose several promising directions for future studies.

papers.title: Integrative Multi-Omics Reveals Differential Mechanisms of Four TCM Formulations in Treating Insomnia via Syndrome-Compound-Metabolite Association Networks.

To elucidate the "same disease, different treatment" mechanisms of these four formulations against sleep deprivation-induced insomnia through an integrated multi-omics and network pharmacology strategy. Chemical constituents were characterized by UHPLC-Orbitrap-MS/MS. A meta-analysis evaluated clinical differences and syndrome consistency. Subsequently, A mouse model of sleep deprivation was established; behavioral tests and HE/Nissl staining were performed. On this basis, fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, serum metabolomics, and hypothalamic transcriptomics were integrated to construct a microbiota-metabolite network. Furthermore, network pharmacology and molecular docking predicted component-target interactions. Finally, key protein expression was validated by western blot. UHPLC-Orbitrap-MS/MS identified 87, 56, 163, and 128 compounds from GPW, WLC, BLMC, and ZRASC, respectively. Syndrome-efficacy interactions were inconsistent. In mice, all formulations alleviated neuronal damage despite heterogeneous behavioral improvements. In this study, these four formulations showed heterogeneous, syndrome-associated patterns across microbiota remodeling, metabolic reprogramming, anti-inflammation, and anti-ferroptosis, which may help generate hypotheses regarding the "same disease, different treatment" principle. Standardized mean differences (SMD) were estimated for outcomes using random-effects models. Subgroup differences between EMIs and JITAIs were tested, and sensitivity analyses were conducted. papers.title: Developmental trajectories of pain empathy: evidence from drift diffusion modeling and EEG time-frequency analysis.
papers.abstract: Pain empathy develops from childhood into adulthood, but the cognitive and neural processes that support this development remain incompletely understood. The present study analyzed behavioral and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 120 participants (children, adolescents, and adults) who completed an Attention-to-Pain-Cue (A-P) task and an Attention-to-Non-Pain-Cue (A-N) task with painful and non-painful limb images. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (HDDM) was used to characterize latent decision processes, and EEG time-frequency analyses were used to examine alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Across alternative DDM specifications, children showed lower drift rates, wider decision boundaries when averaged across image types, and longer non-decision times than older participants, which could be interpreted as differences in domain-general decision dynamics within pain-related task contexts. The EEG results showed age-related differences in alpha- and beta-band ERD, with reduced neural differentiation between painful and non-painful stimuli in children when pain cues were task-irrelevant. Together, these findings suggest that pain-related processing across development is shaped by both general maturation of decision processes and the increasing ability to maintain neural sensitivity to pain cues under changing attentional demands.

papers.title: Volume status as a potential state-dependent modifier of obstructive sleep apnea severity in chronic kidney disease and dialysis: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: This narrative review examines whether volume status may act as an underrecognized, state-dependent modifier of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and dialysis-dependent kidney failure. The main question was which links between extracellular volume, rostral fluid shift, and OSA are supported by empirical studies, and which implications for assessment and treatment remain hypothesis-generating. Evidence was synthesized from thematic searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026, supplemented by reference-list review. An integrative narrative approach used purposive study selection and qualitative interpretation rather than systematic screening, pooled analysis, or formal risk-of-bias assessment. Sleep apnea is common in CKD and end-stage kidney disease, particularly when objective testing is used. Small physiological and imaging studies, mainly in hemodialysis patients, associate fluid overload and regional fluid measures with sleep apnea severity. Responses to fluid removal are heterogeneous, and some intervention studies include both obstructive and central events. These findings do not establish a reproducible volume-sensitive OSA phenotype. Effects on sleep-study timing, positive airway pressure (PAP) requirements, residual events, drug-induced sleep endoscopy, and upper-airway intervention outcomes remain unestablished. Volume status is a plausible state-dependent modifier of OSA severity in selected patients, supported predominantly by small dialysis studies. Distinguishing systemic from regional fluid and transient measurement states from reproducible patient characteristics provides a framework for testable hypotheses. Current evidence does not justify changes to sleep-study scheduling, PAP management, or upper-airway treatment selection.

papers.title: Identification and validation of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for endometriosis through integrating machine learning and single-cell analysis.
papers.abstract: Endometriosis (EMs) is a chronic inflammatory disease, and the lack of candidate molecular biomarkers remain a major clinical challenge. Circadian rhythm disruption plays a non-negligible role in EMs. However, the diagnostic potential of circadian rhythm-related biomarkers remains insufficiently validated. We performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis to screen for endometriosis-related hub modules. Four machine learning algorithms were used for feature selection in the training cohort, and the resulting diagnostic model was evaluated in three independent GEO validation cohorts. To evaluate the immune microenvironment, we applied MCPcounter, CIBERSORT, and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. Single‑cell RNA‑seq data were processed with Seurat for cell clustering and annotation, cell‑cell communication networks were constructed using CellChat, and pseudotime trajectory analysis was performed with Monocle. SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS were identified as candidate molecular biomarkers, demonstrating favorable diagnostic performance across three independent validation sets. Computational immune infiltration analysis suggested higher enrichment scores for B cells and CD8+ T cells, along with lower scores for Tregs and NK cells in EMs samples. Single-cell analysis revealed an increased proportion of mesenchymal cells in EMs samples and altered cell-cell communication involving BMP, CHEMERIN, and GRN signaling pathways. Pseudotime analysis further suggested transcriptional relationships among distinct stromal cell populations. This study identified SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS as candidate tissue-based molecular biomarkers for EMs and revealed alterations in stromal cell populations and immune-related features associated with the disease.

papers.title: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline and drug-induced encephalopathy secondary to teprotumumab for thyroid eye disease: a case report and narrative literature review.
papers.abstract: Teprotumumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R), is an approved targeted therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is an extremely rare but potentially severe central nervous system adverse event, with only three cases reported globally to date. We report the first Han-Chinese patient with Graves' disease and associated TED complicated by teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy, together with a narrative review of all published cases, to raise clinicians' awareness and improve early recognition and management of this rare complication. A 56-year-old Chinese man with Graves' disease and TED developed acute progressive apathy and encephalopathy characterised by multidomain cognitive and behavioral dysfunction 20 days after the third teprotumumab infusion, with an admission MMSE score of 15. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening were unremarkable. Prolonged video-electroencephalography(VEEG) demonstrated intermittent diffuse bilateral slow-wave activity, and widespread interictal epileptiform discharges without electrographic or clinical seizures. Systematic workup excluded infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and psychiatric encephalopathy. Treatment-emergent hyperglycemia was confirmed as a secondary aggravating factor rather than the primary cause. The patient achieved prominent neurological recovery after individualized treapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) and symptomatic management, with a Naranjo score of 6 indicating probable drug-related encephalopathy. Synthesis of all three previously published teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy cases demonstrates that neurological toxicity can develop as early as the third infusion cycle. These cases present consistent neuroimaging features with variable CSF profiles, and thyroid autoantibody elevation predominantly reflects pre-existing Graves' disease-related autoimmune background instead of directly mediating neurotoxicity. TPE generally facilitates neurological recovery but may be complicated by procedural hypersensitivity and fluctuating therapeutic responses. Notably, interictal epileptiform discharges on VEEG represent a newly identified neurophysiological manifestation of this rare adverse event. A three-hit interacting pathogenic hypothesis is proposed: impaired IGF-1R-dependent neurotrophic signalling serves as the core injury mechanism, while underlying thyroid autoimmunity and treatment-related metabolic disturbance act as susceptibility-modifying factors. This case expands the ethnic and clinical spectrum of teprotumumab-related encephalopathy. Diffuse interictal epileptiform discharges without ictal changes reflect reactive cortical hyperexcitability secondary to acute encephalopathy. Metabolic disturbance merely exacerbated neurological impairment. Limitations include single-case constraints, simultaneous multi-intervention therapy, and lack of direct intracranial mechanistic evidence. Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is a rare but serious adverse event. Close neurological surveillance and are essential during medication. Accumulated cases are needed to establish unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.

papers.title: A Kampo medicine, kamishoyosan, ameliorates menstruation-associated symptoms in patients with premenstrual syndrome: An exploratory open-label, randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a psychological or physical symptom. We conducted an open-label, randomized, exploratory trial with the aim of evaluating the efficacy and safety of kamishoyosan (KSS) for PMS. KSS was administered orally during three menstrual cycles. The primary endpoint was the change in the premenstrual Menstrual Distress Questionnaire (MDQ) total score. The secondary endpoints included MDQ total and subscale scores, a daily symptom questionnaire, the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) Questionnaire, overall impressions, sleep status, and heart rate. A total of 50 patients were enrolled. The primary endpoint, the premenstrual MDQ total score, was significantly ameliorated after KSS treatment. Furthermore, KSS reduced MDQ scores during the menstrual cycle. Among the MDQ subscales, KSS decreased score of pain, concentration, behavioral change, and negative feelings during the premenstrual cycle. In addition, hyperthymia reduced during the menstrual cycle. The only adverse event related to KSS was headache in one case. These exploratory findings suggest that KSS may improve menstrual-related symptoms in PMS.

papers.title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.

papers.title: Neuromodulatory effects of audio-proprio-phonatory reinforcement training on subjective tinnitus, a HD-EEG study protocol.
papers.abstract: Tinnitus affects 14% of the global population, with 2% experiencing a severe form of the condition. Sound therapy using white noise emitted by hearing aids is a common intervention, supported by the phenomenon of residual inhibition observed during tinnitus assessment. This study aims to investigate whether audio-proprio-phonatory reinforcement training can improve the quality of life of patients with chronic subjective tinnitus by enabling them to listen to their own phonation, which may mask the tinnitus or induce residual inhibition. We will conduct a prospective, controlled, monocentric, 2-arm block-randomized study, stratified by the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) score, involving two groups for two sequential phases (Phase 1 and Phase 2). Fifty-six patients with tinnitus, recruited from the Ear Nose Throat (ENT) Department of Orléans University Hospital, will undergo a five-week training program, randomized into weekly remote group workshops, and daily individual sessions using specially developed videos. Training efficacy will be assessed through self-report questionnaires. The primary endpoint, the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, will be assessed at three ENT medical visits: at inclusion, end of phase 1 and end of phase 2. Additionally, patients in both groups will regularly complete Visual Analog Scales for Tinnitus and five related questions (noise, cervical, jaw, sleep, stress-anxiety) via a secure digital platform throughout the study. High-density electroencephalograms (HD-EEG) will be performed in a blinded manner before and after Phase 1 at the Neurology Department of Orléans University Hospital. This pilot study aims to evaluate the clinical efficacy of audio-proprio-phonatory training in patients with chronic subjective tinnitus and to objectively measure its effects using HD-EEG. We will explore potential correlations between changes brain activity (such as functional brain connectivity) and clinical responses to the intervention.

papers.title: "It Just Puts You Out!" 'Tranq Sleep,' Sensory Discernment, and the Experience of Consuming Xylazine-Adulterated Fentanyl in Rural North Carolina.
papers.abstract: Xylazine, a veterinary sedative not approved for human use, has emerged as a consequential adulterant in the U.S. illicit fentanyl supply. Although a growing body of qualitative research has documented the experiences of fentanyl consumers exposed to 'tranq' in large Northeastern cities, little is known about how xylazine is experienced in rural or Southern regions where the evolution of the illicit drug supply often lags behind its urban equivalents. This study examines how fentanyl consumers in west-central North Carolina detect, comprehend and respond to the widespread adulteration of fentanyl markets with xylazine. Between September and December of 2025, a seasoned interviewer conducted 25 in-depth, semi-structured qualitative interviews with fentanyl consumers recruited from both fixed and mobile syringe service programs in west-central North Carolina. Interviews explored sensory discernment strategies, pharmacologic effects, and behavioral responses to the presence of xylazine. Data were analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach in QSR NVivo 14.0. Participants described a distinctive repertoire of sensory strategies for identifying xylazine in their fentanyl supply, including the appearance of drug residue on foil, bitterness and chemical odor when smoked, and altered viscosity when injected. A minority described an inability to detect xylazine through sensory cues. Participants consistently distinguished a profound involuntary sedation they called "tranq sleep" from the familiar opioid nod, characterizing it by nearly instantaneous loss of consciousness with severe withdrawal upon awakening. While nearly all participants expressed strong aversion to xylazine, a meaningful minority valued its amplifying effects to 'improve' a diminishing fentanyl high. This study offers among the first qualitative description of xylazine exposure in a rural fentanyl market. Findings extend the xylazine literature geographically and pharmacologically and underscore the urgency of harm reduction responses tailored to the distinctive harms of xylazine. papers.title: Lineage-specific histories rather than shared drivers shape olfactory evolution in New World monkeys
papers.abstract: Variation in primate olfactory receptor gene repertoires has been linked to shared ecological and sensory drivers, including diet, diurnality, and colour vision. Yet within anthropoids, each link rests on a single lineage, leaving unclear whether this variation reflects a shared response to these drivers or lineage-specific histories. Here, we combine genomic data from 80 New World monkey species with CT-based olfactory anatomy and ecological data to investigate the evolutionary processes underlying repertoire variation. Ecological and sensory variables explain little of this variation; even routinely trichromatic, leaf-eating howler monkeys have repertoires of unremarkable size. Instead, convergent reductions in repertoire size arose through distinct genomic routes: extensive gene inactivation in titi monkeys and large structural deletions in squirrel monkeys. Owl monkeys, the only anthropoids that reverted to nocturnality, retained rather than expanded a large ancestral repertoire shared with diurnal capuchins, and instead enlarged their olfactory bulb. Repertoire size covaries with olfactory bulb volume across the radiation, but only partially within lineages: squirrel monkeys show the converse, losing receptors without a matching bulb reduction. Thus, olfactory evolution in New World monkeys reflects historical contingency rather than a shared response, with convergent changes in repertoire size and partial decoupling of genomic and anatomical evolution.
